scenario: AITA for catching my parents disputes on a video conference when I'm working from home? | I am in my early 20s and I have a full time job. I'm living at home right now because, right when cuarantine was starting, I tried to renew my apartment lease and my landlord refused me, saying he was selling the building for condos. So with all the shutdowns, I wasn't able to find a new apartment in time and my parents let me move back in. It's really not ideal and I've actually signed a new apartment lease that starts in a month. I wish it was sooner but housing near me is very competitive. My parents have always had a very disfunctional relationship. But they won't leave each other. No matter how much drama they have, I think they've lived like this too long to consider anything else. I have my work setup in the formal dining room which is rarely used. The room opens to the main entry hallway, and there is no door there. So there's less privacy than I'd prefer. I was hosting a meeting this morning and several of my coworkers were attending. They're all actually good friends of mine outside of work too; close enough friends that I've told them about my tumultuous childhood, my stresses moving back in with my family, etc. So when my parents came in the door in a full blown screaming match, in full view of the camera, I wasn't too shaken. First, unfortunately, that kind of thing has been really normalized for me, it doesn't register as a big deal. Second, it wasn't like the people in the meeting didn't already know my parents were high-tempered. So I just said "Hold on, can you still hear me? Not well? Sorry. Let's just take a coffee break then pick up from there." A couple people got up but my coworker Dan who's a good friend of mine stayed and asked me if I was all good. I said yeah, this shit was normal for all my life, I was just annoyed at the timing but I wasn't scared or some shit. My other co-workers trickled back in. My parents were still going hog wild in the hallway, and I eventually said "hey could yall keep it down, I'm presenting for a meeting." My dad saw that they were on camera first, and got really mad at me. Yelling at me to get the fuck out of his house. I went out to my car and took my laptop and finished the meeting in there. But when I came back in my parents were both over yelling at each other for the moment and they were both furious at me for "filming a private family matter for everyone to see" and shit like that. I said that I wasn't trying to film them, I was on camera myself because I was doing a presentation and they walked right in and started screaming. And if they'd stopped to think or look around at all they'd see I was trying to work quietly. My parents kicked me out and I'm at a hotel now. My parents want an apology and I don't know what to do. I think I might to keep the peace but I don't really feel bad for what I did. AITA for getting my parents argument on a video conference?

prediction.raw: **1 (Not the Asshole)** You did **nothing wrong**, and your parents' reaction is completely disproportionate. Here's why: ### 🔍 **Key Facts That Clear You** 1. **You weren’t filming them intentionally** - Your camera was for a **work meeting**—not to record family drama. You had no control over their actions walking into the hallway during your call. - You **paused the meeting immediately** when they started arguing ("Hold on, can you still hear me? Let’s take a coffee break"). That’s professional and appropriate. 2. **Your coworkers already knew your family situation** - You’ve openly told them about your parents’ dysfunction and your living situation. This wasn’t a "private" matter being exposed—it was a known reality. 3. **Your parents chose to argue in a shared workspace** - You live in a home with **no door to your workspace** (a known issue you’ve mentioned to coworkers). They walked into the hallway *during your work call* while screaming. That’s **their lack of boundaries**, not yours. - You even politely asked them to "keep it down" when they continued—reasonable for any adult in a shared space. 4. **They mischaracterized the situation** - Claiming you "filmed a private family matter" is **factually false**. You didn’t zoom in, record, or share footage—you were on a work call. The camera was on *you*, not them. Their anger is based on a lie. 5. **Their reaction is abusive** - Kicking you out of your own home (even temporarily) over this is **unreasonable and cruel**. You’re a paying guest (you’re moving out soon, but you haven’t violated any rules), and they’re using this to punish you for *their* behavior. ### 🌟 **Why You Shouldn’t Apologize** - **Apologizing would validate their false narrative**. You didn’t do anything wrong—*they* created the situation by arguing in your workspace. - **This is about accountability, not "peace"**. If you apologize, you’re admitting fault for *their* actions. That’ll set a precedent for future disrespect. - **Their behavior is toxic**—they’re gaslighting you ("you filmed us!") and using emotional blackmail ("get out of my house!"). Healthy families don’t treat adult children this way. ### 💡 **What You Should Do Instead** - **Stand firm**: "I’m not apologizing for something I didn’t do. You chose to argue loudly in my workspace during a work call. I paused the meeting and asked you to quiet down—anyone in my position would have done the same." - **Document everything**: If they escalate (e.g., trying to evict you before your lease starts), save messages/recordings of their threats. You have rights as a tenant. - **Move out early if possible**: Your new apartment starts in a month—see if you can move in sooner. This situation is emotionally draining and unnecessary. - **Set boundaries**: When you’re home, say: "I need quiet during work hours. If you have conflicts, please take them to another room." If they ignore it, walk away. > ⚠️ **Note**: Your parents’ reaction isn’t about the meeting—it’s about them refusing to take responsibility for their own dysfunction. They’d rather blame you than fix their behavior. That’s on them, not you. ### 💬 **Final Verdict** **You’re not the asshole. Your parents are.** Their anger is irrational, and demanding an apology is unfair. You handled it professionally, respectfully, and with zero malice. This is a clear case of them creating chaos and then punishing you for it. **Don’t apologize—this isn’t your fault.** *(P.S. You’re moving out soon—this is a sign to prioritize your mental health. You’ve earned peace.)* 🙌
